title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary-school English as a foreign language (EFL) students use generative AI text when composing writing, and whether particular patterns of human-AI text integration are associated with better writing quality. The authors frame the study around concerns that AI may both support writing and distort students’ demonstrated proficiency, especially when students rely heavily on AI-generated text. The research questions focus on the linguistic features of AI-generated text embedded in student compositions, the interaction patterns students use with AI-generated text, and whether these patterns benefit different types of learners differently.

The study analyzed 59 compositions written by Hong Kong secondary school students from seven schools with different academic achievement profiles. Students attended a two-hour workshop on attempting a writing task with ChatGPT support, learned either a genre-based or process-based writing approach plus prompt engineering, and then completed a feature article task within two weeks. Students were required to include both their own words and AI-generated text, and to self-highlight which portions came from chatbots. The researchers then conducted content analysis of the compositions, multiple linear regression examining associations between text features and scores, and cluster analysis to identify learner profiles and interaction patterns.

Across the sample, compositions relied heavily on AI text: on average, 63.39% of words were AI-generated, and many compositions contained 70% or more AI-generated text. The main quantitative finding was that total word count—whether AI-generated or human-written—was the strongest predictor of writing scores, whereas the particular chunking pattern of AI text was generally less predictive. However, this relationship differed by academic profile. Students from higher-banding schools appeared better able to benefit from either AI-generated or human-authored words and were more capable of writing independently. In contrast, students from lower-banding schools often relied more heavily on AI-generated text, and revising AI output with their own words was sometimes associated with lower scores.

The authors conclude that generative AI can enhance EFL writing, but benefits are uneven and depend on students’ preexisting writing competence and AI literacy. Higher-achieving students seem better positioned to use AI strategically to support writing, while lower-achieving students may become more dependent on AI without gaining comparable improvement in writing quality. The paper argues that educators should emphasize independent writing ability, process-writing skills, and effective prompting so that AI enhances rather than replaces student writing effort.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical K-12 study with clear methods, human-rated outcomes, and statistical analyses, but it is observational/correlational without a control group or causal identification strategy. It provides direct secondary-school evidence but only meets limited causal credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially beneficial but heterogeneous associations between generative AI-supported writing and literacy outcomes, with clear tradeoffs by student achievement level and no standardized causal effect size. Overall impact is promising but unclear and uneven, especially for lower-achieving students.

interventions.use_case: Secondary school EFL students used ChatGPT and other generative AI chatbots to co-compose a feature article by integrating AI-generated text with their own writing, including drafting and revision in a machine-in-the-loop writing process.
Students interacted with conversational generative AI chatbots through prompt engineering to generate writing content and support idea development and revision during article composition.

finding.finding_summary: In 59 Hong Kong secondary EFL students composing feature articles with AI support, overall writing quality was mainly predicted by total number of words, whether AI- or human-generated; partial correlations between total score and AI words (0.417, p<0.01) and human words (0.424, p<0.01) were positive. However, benefits differed by learner profile: for students from high-banding schools, scores were more strongly associated with both AI and human word counts (e.g., total score partial correlations 0.578 and 0.544, both p<0.01), whereas for low-banding schools AI word count was not significantly associated with higher scores and human revision of AI text was associated with lower content/organization performance.
finding.measure: Human-rated HKDSE feature article writing scores: content, language, organization, and total score; composition structure including AI-generated vs human-written words and chunks
finding.effect_size: partial correlations reported (e.g., total score with AI words r=0.417; with human words r=0.424; high-band subgroup total score with AI words r=0.578; with human words r=0.544)
finding.std_deviation: Total score SD=3.28; Content SD=1.27; Language SD=1.02; Organization SD=1.10

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests students differed in their ability to independently draft, revise, and strategically integrate AI-generated text, indicating variation in process-writing and AI-literacy-related skills. Cluster analyses identified profiles with high scores under either high or low AI use, but low-achieving students appeared less proficient at revising AI output and more dependent on verbatim AI text, implying uneven development of self-regulated writing and evaluative judgment; no standardized durable-skills effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Observed interaction patterns with AI-generated text, prompt use, chunk integration, and inferred drafting/revision strategy quality from regression and cluster analysis
